title: Who are truly the uneducated
source_text: Καίτοι γε ἄλλους μέν φησιν ἀπαιδευτοτάτους εἶναι καὶ ἀνδράποδα καὶ ἀμαθεστάτους ὁ Κέλσος, τοὺς μὴ ἐπισταμένους αὐτοῦ τὰ προστάγματα μηδὲ παιδευθέντας τὰ Ἑλλήνων μαθήματα· ἡμεῖς δὲ ἀπαιδευτοτάτους φαμὲν τοὺς μὴ αἰσχυνομένους ἐν τῷ τοῖς ἀψύχοις προσλαλεῖν καὶ περὶ μὲν ὑγείας τὸ ἀσθενὲς ἐπικαλουμένους περὶ δὲ ζωῆς τὸ νεκρὸν ἀξιοῦντας περὶ δ᾿ ἐπικουρίας τὸ ἀπορώτατον ἱκετεύοντας. κἄν τινες δὲ μὴ ταῦτα φῶσιν εἶναι τοὺς θεοὺς ἀλλὰ μιμήματα τῶν ἀληθινῶν κἀκείνων σύμβολα. οὐδὲν ἧττον καὶ οὗτοι. ἐν βαναύσων χερσὶ τὰ μιμήματα τῆς θειότητος φανταζόμενοι εἶναι. ἀπαίδευτοί εἰσι καὶ ἀνδράποδα καὶ ἀμαθεῖς· ὡς τοὺς ἐσχάτους τῶν ἐν ἡμῖν ἀπηλλάχθαι ταύτης τῆς ἀπαιδευσίας καὶ τῆς ἀμαθίας, καὶ φρονιμωτάτοις δὲ τὴν θείαν ἐλπίδα νοεῖσθαι καὶ καταλαμβάνεσθαί φαμεν. λέγομεν δὲ καὶ οὐχ οἷόν τ᾿ εἶναι μὴ ἐγγυμνασάμενον τῇ ἀνθρωπίνῃ σοφίᾳ χωρεῖν τὴν θειοτέραν, καὶ μωρίαν πᾶσαν τὴν ἀνθρωπίνην σοφίαν ὡς πρὸς τὴν θείαν ὁμολογοῦμεν. εἶτα δέον αὐτὸν ἀγωνίζεσθαι περὶ τοῦ λόγου, ὁ δὲ γόητας ἡμᾶς καλεῖ καί φησιν ὅτί φεύγομεν τοὺς χαριεστέρους προτροπάδην ὡς οὐχ ἑτοίμους ἀπατᾶσθαι. παλεύομεν δὲ τοὺς ἀγροικοτέρους. οὐ γὰρ εἶδεν ἄνωθεν καὶ ἐξ ἀρχῆς καὶ τοῖς ἔξωθεν μαθήμασι πεπαιδευμένους τοὺς παρ᾿ ἡμῖν σοφοὺς, Μωϋσέα μὲν „πάσῃ Αἰγυπτίων σοφίᾳ,“ Δανιὴλ δὲ καὶ Ἀνανίαν καὶ Ἀζαρίαν καὶ Μισαὴλ πᾶσι τοῖς Ἀσσυρίων γράμμασιν, ὥστ᾿ αὐτοὺς εὑρεθῆναι πάντων τῶν ἐκεῖ σοφῶν δεκαπλασίους. καὶ νῦν δὲ αἱ ἐκκλησίαι ἔχουσι μὲν ἀνάλογον τοῖς πλήθεσιν ὀλίγους σοφοὺς προσελθόντας καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς καλουμένης παρ᾿ ἡμῖν „κατὰ σάρκα“ σοφίας, ἔχουσι δὲ καὶ τοὺς διαβεβηκότας ἀπ᾿ ἐκείνης ἐπὶ τὴν θείαν σοφίαν.
pass_a_gloss: And yet Celsus says others (ἄλλους μέν) are most uneducated and slaves (ἀνδράποδα) and most ignorant (ἀμαθέστατοι), those not knowing his injunctions (προστάγματα) nor educated in the learnings (μαθήματα) of the Greeks; but we say most uneducated those not ashamed (αἰσχυνομένους) at addressing (προσλαλεῖν) lifeless things (ἄψυχα), and calling upon the weak (ἀσθενές) about health (ὑγεία), asking (ἀξιοῦντας) the dead (νεκρόν) about life (ζωή), supplicating (ἱκετεύοντας) the most resourceless/helpless (ἀπορώτατον) about aid (ἐπικουρία). And even if some say these are not the gods but imitations (μιμήματα) of the true ones and symbols (σύμβολα) of those, no less these too, imagining (φανταζόμενοι) the imitations of the deity (θειότης) to be in the hands of mechanics (βάναυσοι), are uneducated and slaves and ignorant; so that (ὡς) we say the last/least (ἔσχατοι) of those among us have been freed (ἀπηλλάχθαι) from this lack of education (ἀπαιδευσία) and ignorance (ἀμαθία), and the divine hope (ἐλπίς) is understood (νοεῖσθαι) and grasped by the most intelligent (φρονιμώτατοι). And we say also that it is not possible for one not trained (ἐγγυμνασάμενον) in human wisdom to contain (χωρεῖν) the more divine, and we confess (ὁμολογοῦμεν) all human wisdom foolishness as compared with (ὡς πρός) the divine. Then, though he ought to contend (ἀγωνίζεσθαι) about the argument, he calls us sorcerers/charlatans (γόητες) and says that we flee headlong (προτροπάδην) the more refined (χαριέστεροι) as not ready to be deceived (ἀπατᾶσθαι), but lure like birds (παλεύομεν) the more rustic (ἀγροικότεροι). For he did not see that from of old (ἄνωθεν) and from the beginning our wise men were educated also in outside learnings, Moses 'in all wisdom of the Egyptians', and Daniel and Ananias and Azarias and Misael in all the letters (γράμματα) of the Assyrians, so that they were found tenfold (δεκαπλάσιοι) of all the wise there. And now also the churches have, in proportion (ἀνάλογον) to the multitudes (πλήθη), few wise who have come (προσελθόντας) even from the wisdom called among us 'according to the flesh (κατὰ σάρκα)', and have also those who have passed over (διαβεβηκότας) from that to the divine wisdom.
pass_b_english: It is true that Celsus calls one set of people “most uneducated and slaves and most ignorant”: those who do not know his precepts and have not been schooled in the learning of the Greeks. We, however, call most uneducated those who are not ashamed to talk to lifeless things, who call on what is weak for health, ask what is dead for life, and beg what is most helpless for help (Wisdom of Solomon 13:17–18). And even if some say that these things are not the gods but imitations and symbols of the true ones, these too are none the less uneducated and slaves and ignorant, since they imagine that imitations of the divine are in the hands of common craftsmen. So we say that even the least among us have been freed from this lack of education and this ignorance, and that the divine hope is understood and grasped by the most intelligent.

We also say that it is impossible for one who has not been trained in human wisdom to take in the more divine wisdom; and we confess that all human wisdom is foolishness compared with the divine. Then, when he ought to argue the point, he calls us charlatans and says that we flee headlong from the more cultivated, since they are not ready to be deceived, and lure in the more rustic like birds. For he did not see that from the very beginning our wise men were schooled in outside learning as well: Moses “in all the wisdom of the Egyptians” (Acts 7:22), and Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael in all the learning of the Assyrians, so that they were found ten times better than all the wise men there (Daniel 1:4, 17, 20). Even now the churches have, in proportion to their numbers, few wise men who have come to them from what we call wisdom “according to the flesh” (1 Corinthians 1:26); but they also have those who have passed from that wisdom to the divine wisdom.

choices.choice: The description of idol-worshippers echoes Wisdom of Solomon 13:17–18 closely (not ashamed to speak to a lifeless thing; for health calls on the weak; for life asks the dead; for help entreats...); Origen has ἀπορώτατον (‘most helpless’) where the LXX has ἀπειρότατον (‘most inexperienced’). The three labels in the first sentence are Celsus’s own (quoted); ‘his precepts’ (αὐτοῦ τὰ προστάγματα) are Celsus’s teachings. Celsus’s charge that ‘we flee headlong from the more cultivated... and decoy the more boorish’ is reported by Origen in the first person plural (φεύγομεν, παλεύομεν), so it is kept as indirect speech without quotation marks; παλεύω is a bird-catcher’s word (‘lure with a decoy’), hence ‘lure in... like birds’. γόητες rendered ‘charlatans’ (also ‘sorcerers’). Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael are the English Bible forms of Origen’s Ananias, Azarias, Misael (order kept as in the Greek). The ‘Assyrians’ is Origen’s word; Daniel 1:4 speaks of the learning (γράμματα) of the Chaldeans, 1:17 of skill in all learning, 1:20 of being found ten times better; all three are cited inline. ἀγροικότεροι rendered ‘more rustic’ (Celsus’s contrast is refined against rustic, not polite against rude). Wisdom ‘according to the flesh’ echoes 1 Corinthians 1:26 (‘not many wise according to the flesh’).

'can be in the hands of common craftsmen' changed to 'are' (no modal in φανταζόμενοι εἶναι)
'want of education' (archaic) changed to 'lack of education'
